brands.name: Tom Wegener Surfboards
brands.short_description: Master shaper Tom Wegener — cork-core wood and performance surfboards from Noosa, from alaias and noseriders to the Model A learner shape.

models.name: Noserider
models.description: For a long time the goal for noseriders has been to adjust the rocker while on the nose. While hanging five or ten, you flatten the rocker, or even get reverse rocker, adding another level of speed and control. This was the idea behind the stringerless boards of the late 1960s. The feel was good but the materials were not right. The glassed, stringerless boards broke and lost their spring. The Corky method has allowed me to get the flex that has been the sort of holy grail for noseriders.

models.name: 12' Sunday Glider
models.description: I have really spent a lot of time on 12 plus surfboards. This is going to sound silly, but I see the 12 footer as the very short end of the spectrum of longboards. Longboards are from 12 to 20 feet long. This is where my shapes are different from others. The aquadynamics come from a different paradigm. I pull the centre of volume back from the midpoint because I want the sweet spot to be back to tighten the turning radius.

models.name: Model A
models.description: The Model A is the best Surfboard for learning how to surf. It is geared for catching waves easily and early, and then having control through the drop. This is the critical moment for the beginner to mid-level surfer — where it is make or break. The Model A makes the answer "surf" as the surfer glides toward the shoulder and finds trim. But it is not only a beginner board, it noserides well.

models.name: Finless Corkys
models.description: I use the analogy of driving a car to demonstrate the difference between finned and finless surfing. With a finned board all four wheels of the car are secure on the road when turning. With finless the four wheels are sliding as you drift around every corner and then accelerate out of the turn with a spring as the tires grab the road — or as the rails reengage with the wave.

models.name: Fish and Mid-Lengths
models.description: The corky method has opened the door to new feels and rides for fish and mid-lengths. I vary the flex, spring and weight of the boards and there are lots of variations. I can make them very light and rigid which makes them quick to turn and respond. Or, I can make them with flex through the board giving drive and gouging turns.

models.name: Toothpick
models.description: If I could have only two surfboards, one would be an alaia and one would be a toothpick. The toothpick glides across a swell better than any other board I have known. The finesse and elegance of sliding into a swell way outside the impact zone on a long hollow plywood board is surreal.

models.name: Ancient Hawaiian Olo
models.description: The Olo surfboard was reserved for the ancient Hawaiian royal class. Surfing as the "sport of kings" comes from stand-up surfing by the royalty of Hawaii surfing on the long Olo surfboards.

models.name: Albacore
models.description: I designed the Albacore in 2009 and now I am expanding on this design with the corky method. I have surfed wood surfboards for a long time. In 1981-82 I was riding three balsa longboards and I loved their glide and liveliness.

models.name: Alaia
models.description: The Alaia is a thin wood surfboard used by the ancient Hawaiians. Although it was their most popular surfboard for hundreds of years, it virtually disappeared from history for the entire 20th century. Because the surfboard is very thin, never more than one inch thick, it is difficult to paddle and without fins it was thought that it could not angle across a wave.
